newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Red Cross considers armed guards to boost security.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross considers armed guards to boost security.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross said on Thursday it planned armed protection for its staff after losing nine employees in brutal attacks in 1996.
The Swiss-run humanitarian agency said that in response to declining respect for its emblem, it was considering measures to boost staff security in conflict zones, including armed guards.
The ICRC lost six Western employees in Chechnya and another three in Burundi in terrorist attacks in 1996, the highest number of such deaths in its 133-year history.

The six medical staff in Chechnya were shot dead in their sleep in a hospital compound by armed gunmen in December. The agency said it still did not know who was behind the attack. Three Swiss staff were killed in an ambush last June in Burundi.
The ICRC's deputy chief of operations Jacques Stroun said practical protection measures were needed in the field.
Security was high on the agenda this week when ICRC held its first-ever meeting of 55 heads of delegation amid soul-searching in the agency over its future mandate.
The ICRC, with more than 8,000 workers, takes a leading role in enforcing international law governing the use of weapons in war, treatment of prisoners and civilians.

It looks after the sick, traces lost children, visits prisoners, helps mine victims, feeds the hungry and saves lives in the frontline of emergencies from east Zaire, Rwanda and Somalia to ex-Yugoslavia, Tajikistan and Afghanistan.
Its humanitarian work depends on its neutrality and fragile trust. It does not take sides in political, racial, religious or ideological conflicts and cherishes its independence.
But the lives of ICRC workers are often at risk in dangerous and isolated war zones, said ICRC security chief Philippe Dind.
"We will reinforce physical passive protection measures...We wish to use armed guards in proportion to the external danger to protect our people in their residences and offices," he said.
Dind ruled out armed guards for staff on the move. He did not say what kind of guards would be deployed and when.
Rwanda was one country where the ICRC was considering using armed guards after the brutal murder of three Spanish aid workers of the agency Medecins du Monde on Saturday, he added.
Armed protection would be a departure from the ICRC's reliance on its impartiality and its emblem for protection.
Stroun said the agency needed to study new economic and political factors in war zones, where conflicts were becoming more complex and players more numerous.
"Today's classic picture is no longer like the one in France or Germany after the (Second World) War, he said.

"We need knowledge. We plan to hire an economist specialised in war economy...One of our objectives is to make contact with academics working in this field. There's need for bigger debate among all humanitarian agencies to reduce security risks."
